introduction: This level focuses on the quantitative relationships in chemical reactions (Stoichiometry) and the preparation of solutions. It introduces the critical concept of the Limiting Reagent and the various ways to express the concentration of a solute in a solvent.

core_concepts.title: Empirical and Molecular Formula
core_concepts.description:
1. Empirical Formula: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of various elements present in a molecule. 
2. Molecular Formula: The exact number of atoms of various elements present in a molecule. 
Relation: $\text{Molecular Formula} = (\text{Empirical Formula})_n$, where $n = \frac{\text{Molecular Mass}}{\text{Empirical Formula Mass}}$.

core_concepts.title: Stoichiometry and Limiting Reagent (LR)
core_concepts.description:
Stoichiometry deals with the mass-volume relationships based on a BALANCED chemical equation. The Limiting Reagent (LR) is the reactant that is completely consumed first in a reaction, thereby strictly dictating the maximum amount of product formed. The Excess Reagent (ER) is the reactant left over. 
**Trick to find LR**: Divide the given moles of each reactant by its stoichiometric coefficient from the balanced equation. The reactant with the smallest resulting ratio is the Limiting Reagent.

core_concepts.title: Temperature-Dependent Concentration Terms
core_concepts.description:
These involve Volume, which expands/contracts with temperature: 
1. Molarity ($M$): Moles of solute per Liter of solution ($M = n/V_{\text{in L}}$). 
2. Percentage weight by volume ($\%, w/v$): Mass of solute (g) per $100 \text{ mL}$ of solution. 
3. Normality ($N$): Number of gram-equivalents of solute per Liter of solution (covered deeply in Level 3).

core_concepts.title: Temperature-Independent Concentration Terms
core_concepts.description:
These involve Mass, which does not change with temperature: 
1. Molality ($m$): Moles of solute per Kilogram of solvent (Note: SOLVENT, not solution). $m = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{W_{\text{solvent in kg}}}$. 
2. Mole Fraction ($x_A$): Ratio of moles of component A to the total moles in the mixture ($x_A = \frac{n_A}{n_A + n_B}$). Always, $\sum x_i = 1$. 
3. Percentage weight by weight ($\%, w/w$): Mass of solute per $100 \text{ g}$ of solution.

important_entities.name: Dilution and Mixing Formulas
important_entities.key_fact: Dilution: $M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2$. Mixing: $M_{\text{final}} = \frac{M_1 V_1 + M_2 V_2}{V_1 + V_2}$.
important_entities.significance: When diluting a solution by adding water, the total MOLES of solute ($M \times V$) remain perfectly constant, hence $M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2$. When mixing two non-reacting solutions of the same substance, the total moles just add up.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Molarity ($M$) uses the Volume of the ENTIRE SOLUTION in its denominator. Molality ($m$) uses the Mass of the SOLVENT ONLY in its denominator. Students frequently use the mass of the entire solution for molality, which yields an incorrect, smaller value. Always subtract the mass of the solute from the mass of the solution to find the mass of the solvent.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: If a question provides the density ($d$ in $\text{g/mL}$) and the mass percentage ($x\%, w/w$) of a solution, you can instantly find its Molarity using the shortcut: $M = \frac{10 \times x \times d}{M_w}$, where $M_w$ is the molar mass of the solute. This skips 3 steps of complex conversions.

exam_strategy_tips: NEVER perform stoichiometric calculations on an unbalanced equation. The stoichiometric coefficients represent the exact mole-to-mole ratios. If the equation isn't balanced, your Limiting Reagent calculation will be entirely wrong.
